answer:
The ocean is salty mostly because of rocks on land. Rainwater is slightly acidic, so it slowly breaks down rock and releases dissolved salts and minerals. Rivers then carry those to the sea [1][3]. Seafloor vents add more: seawater seeps into the crust, gets heated by magma, picks up minerals and flows back out. Underwater volcanic eruptions also release minerals straight into the water [1][3].

Rivers taste fresh because rain keeps refilling them. The ocean is where all those rivers end up, so it collects the salt from every one of them [2]. Water mostly leaves the ocean by evaporating, and the salt doesn't go with it. Over a very long time, that left it at about 3.5% salt by weight, or 35 parts per thousand [3].

Most of that salt is sodium and chloride, the same ingredients as table salt. They make up about 85% of the dissolved ions in seawater according to NOAA, or over 90% according to USGS [1][3]. Today the ocean probably isn't getting any saltier. About as much salt settles to the seafloor as sediment as the rivers bring in [2].
